commit_message:
[WASM] Add platform support, toolchains, and JS proactor. (#24462)

This adds a supported path for building the IREE runtime as a
freestanding wasm32 module. The commit is intentionally
infrastructure-heavy: it teaches Bazel and CMake how to cross-compile
IREE C/C++ targets to wasm32-unknown-unknown, provides the minimal C/JS
runtime surface those targets need, and adds a JavaScript async proactor
so browser/Node integrations can route event-loop completions back into
IREE's async API.

WebGPU is the primary near-term target for browser and JavaScript-hosted
IREE. The HAL work that follows needs a small runtime that can be
embedded in a Web Worker or Node process, instantiate without
Emscripten, exchange buffers and callbacks with JavaScript, and keep the
generated JS companion code tied to the C libraries that declare wasm
imports.

The important product boundary is that this is IREE-owned wasm runtime
infrastructure, not an Emscripten build. That keeps the dependency and
ABI surface small for embedders that already have their own JavaScript
host, allocator, memory ownership rules, or module instantiation path.
It also gives us a direct place to model WebGPU/JS completion behavior
instead of pretending there is a POSIX kernel underneath the browser.

The initial support contract is deliberately single-threaded. This
commit does not claim local-task, pthreads, shared-memory atomics, TLS,
or a thread-safe libc/heap. Those are interesting future directions for
CPU-side wasm+SIMD execution, but WebGPU is the first target and the
current runtime enables only local-sync by default.

* Bazel WebAssembly configuration layered as generic `--config=wasm`
settings plus architecture-specific `--config=wasm32` and
`--config=wasm32_wasi` platforms. The default wasm32 target model uses
`wasm32-unknown-unknown`, freestanding compile/link flags, imported
linear memory, no entry point, and local-sync as the only default HAL
driver.
* A `--config=wasm32_wasi` variant for targets that need
wasi-libc/libc++ behavior such as gtest/gbenchmark-oriented smoke
coverage.
* CMake wasm32 toolchain files mirroring the Bazel target model,
including deterministic wasi-sdk download/cache handling under the build
directory and the same freestanding compile/link flags.
* `iree_wasm_cc_library`, `iree_wasm_entry`, `iree_wasm_cc_binary`, and
`iree_wasm_cc_test` rules/macros for Bazel and CMake. C libraries can
declare JavaScript companion modules in their deps, binaries collect
them transitively, and the bundler emits a single `.mjs` entry point
beside the `.wasm` binary.
* A freestanding wasm libc shim: C headers, dlmalloc-backed allocation,
`sbrk` over `memory.grow`, string/ctype/strtol/stdio/stdlib/unistd
support, and a small `iree_syscall` JavaScript import module for
stdout/stderr, clock, exit, and assertion failure paths.
* Hooks for embedders to bring their own allocator or libc instead of
IREE's defaults. Bazel exposes the generic `--config=custom_allocator`
and `--config=wasm_custom_libc`; CMake exposes `IREE_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM`,
`IREE_WASM_BUILD_IREE_LIBC`, and `IREE_WASM_LIBC_INCLUDE_DIR`.
* JavaScript async proactor support under
`runtime/src/iree/async/platform/js/`. The C proactor owns token tables
and completion dispatch; JavaScript owns the event-loop integration,
Worker/inline entry points, completion ring plumbing, and import modules
used by browser or Node hosts.
* Runtime platform tightening for wasm: target-platform detection,
disabled unsafe synchronization, no threading by default, wasm-safe
time/CSPRNG/sysfs fallbacks, local topology stubs, and build-system
selection of the JS proactor where appropriate.
* Smoke tests for the wasm toolchain, the JS bundler, the JS proactor,
and the token table used to track externally completed operations.
* A small CMake-based `runtime_wasm` CI job that build-checks
representative wasm32 runtime targets with ccache, including a final
wasm link of the real `samples/hal/hello` runtime sample, without
building LLVM, the compiler, host CMake generators, or running
Node-based tests.

Build a freestanding wasm target with Bazel:

    iree-bazel-build \
      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/libc:libc

Run the Bazel bundler smoke test under Node:

    iree-bazel-test \
      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:bundler_test

Use the WASI-flavored platform when a target needs wasi-libc/libc++
rather than IREE's freestanding libc shim:

    iree-bazel-build \
      --config=wasm32_wasi \
      //some:target

Let an embedding application provide libc headers/objects and the
default system allocator:

    iree-bazel-build \
      --config=wasm32 \
      --config=wasm_custom_libc \
      --config=custom_allocator \
      --copt=-DIREE_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM_CTL=my_allocator_ctl \
      //some:target

Configure a CMake wasm32 build with the same target model:

    cmake -B build-wasm -S . \
      -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=build_tools/cmake/wasm32.cmake

Build the CMake runtime wasm subset used by CI:

    cmake --build build-wasm \
      --target \
        iree_wasm_libc \
        iree_samples_hal_hello_hello \
        iree_async_platform_js_proactor \
        iree_hal_drivers_local_sync_sync_driver \
      -- -k 0

Embedders that already provide a libc can disable IREE's libc support or
point the freestanding include path at their own headers:

    cmake -B build-wasm -S . \
      -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=build_tools/cmake/wasm32.cmake \
      -DIREE_WASM_BUILD_IREE_LIBC=OFF \
      -DIREE_WASM_LIBC_INCLUDE_DIR=

from the host, the linked wasm module has no C entry point by default,

disabled because it requires a coherent multithreaded contract across
wasm shared memory, atomics, TLS, stack management, wakeups, and the
allocator/libc. This commit keeps those states unavailable rather than
letting unsupported combinations look accidentally buildable.

not need VMVX or dynamic executable loading, and enabling VMVX today

boundary where they are introduced. Applications with an existing libc

present in the `.wasm` file. This keeps JS host code colocated with the

        iree_hal_drivers_local_sync_sync_driver \

      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:smoke_test \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:bundler_test_bundle \

This adds a supported path for building the IREE runtime as a
freestanding wasm32 module. The commit is intentionally
infrastructure-heavy: it teaches Bazel and CMake how to cross-compile
IREE C/C++ targets to wasm32-unknown-unknown, provides the minimal C/JS
runtime surface those targets need, and adds a JavaScript async proactor
so browser/Node integrations can route event-loop completions back into
IREE's async API.

WebGPU is the primary near-term target for browser and JavaScript-hosted
IREE. The HAL work that follows needs a small runtime that can be
embedded in a Web Worker or Node process, instantiate without
Emscripten, exchange buffers and callbacks with JavaScript, and keep the
generated JS companion code tied to the C libraries that declare wasm
imports.

The important product boundary is that this is IREE-owned wasm runtime
infrastructure, not an Emscripten build. That keeps the dependency and
ABI surface small for embedders that already have their own JavaScript
host, allocator, memory ownership rules, or module instantiation path.
It also gives us a direct place to model WebGPU/JS completion behavior
instead of pretending there is a POSIX kernel underneath the browser.

The initial support contract is deliberately single-threaded. This
commit does not claim local-task, pthreads, shared-memory atomics, TLS,
or a thread-safe libc/heap. Those are interesting future directions for
CPU-side wasm+SIMD execution, but WebGPU is the first target and the
current runtime enables only local-sync by default.

* Bazel WebAssembly configuration layered as generic `--config=wasm`
settings plus architecture-specific `--config=wasm32` and
`--config=wasm32_wasi` platforms. The default wasm32 target model uses
`wasm32-unknown-unknown`, freestanding compile/link flags, imported
linear memory, no entry point, and local-sync as the only default HAL
driver.
* A `--config=wasm32_wasi` variant for targets that need
wasi-libc/libc++ behavior such as gtest/gbenchmark-oriented smoke
coverage.
* CMake wasm32 toolchain files mirroring the Bazel target model,
including deterministic wasi-sdk download/cache handling under the build
directory and the same freestanding compile/link flags.
* `iree_wasm_cc_library`, `iree_wasm_entry`, `iree_wasm_cc_binary`, and
`iree_wasm_cc_test` rules/macros for Bazel and CMake. C libraries can
declare JavaScript companion modules in their deps, binaries collect
them transitively, and the bundler emits a single `.mjs` entry point
beside the `.wasm` binary.
* A freestanding wasm libc shim: C headers, dlmalloc-backed allocation,
`sbrk` over `memory.grow`, string/ctype/strtol/stdio/stdlib/unistd
support, and a small `iree_syscall` JavaScript import module for
stdout/stderr, clock, exit, and assertion failure paths.
* Hooks for embedders to bring their own allocator or libc instead of
IREE's defaults. Bazel exposes the generic `--config=custom_allocator`
and `--config=wasm_custom_libc`; CMake exposes `IREE_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM`,
`IREE_WASM_BUILD_IREE_LIBC`, and `IREE_WASM_LIBC_INCLUDE_DIR`.
* JavaScript async proactor support under
`runtime/src/iree/async/platform/js/`. The C proactor owns token tables
and completion dispatch; JavaScript owns the event-loop integration,
Worker/inline entry points, completion ring plumbing, and import modules
used by browser or Node hosts.
* Runtime platform tightening for wasm: target-platform detection,
disabled unsafe synchronization, no threading by default, wasm-safe
time/CSPRNG/sysfs fallbacks, local topology stubs, and build-system
selection of the JS proactor where appropriate.
* Smoke tests for the wasm toolchain, the JS bundler, the JS proactor,
and the token table used to track externally completed operations.
* A small CMake-based `runtime_wasm` CI job that build-checks
representative wasm32 runtime targets with ccache, including a final
wasm link of the real `samples/hal/hello` runtime sample, without
building LLVM, the compiler, host CMake generators, or running

    iree-bazel-build \
      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/libc:libc

Run the Bazel bundler smoke test under Node:

      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:bundler_test

[WASM] Add platform support, toolchains, and JS proactor. (#24462)

This adds a supported path for building the IREE runtime as a
freestanding wasm32 module. The commit is intentionally
infrastructure-heavy: it teaches Bazel and CMake how to cross-compile
IREE C/C++ targets to wasm32-unknown-unknown, provides the minimal C/JS
runtime surface those targets need, and adds a JavaScript async proactor
so browser/Node integrations can route event-loop completions back into
IREE's async API.

WebGPU is the primary near-term target for browser and JavaScript-hosted
IREE. The HAL work that follows needs a small runtime that can be
embedded in a Web Worker or Node process, instantiate without
Emscripten, exchange buffers and callbacks with JavaScript, and keep the
generated JS companion code tied to the C libraries that declare wasm
imports.

The important product boundary is that this is IREE-owned wasm runtime
infrastructure, not an Emscripten build. That keeps the dependency and
ABI surface small for embedders that already have their own JavaScript
host, allocator, memory ownership rules, or module instantiation path.
It also gives us a direct place to model WebGPU/JS completion behavior
instead of pretending there is a POSIX kernel underneath the browser.

The initial support contract is deliberately single-threaded. This
commit does not claim local-task, pthreads, shared-memory atomics, TLS,
or a thread-safe libc/heap. Those are interesting future directions for
CPU-side wasm+SIMD execution, but WebGPU is the first target and the
current runtime enables only local-sync by default.

* Bazel WebAssembly configuration layered as generic `--config=wasm`
settings plus architecture-specific `--config=wasm32` and
`--config=wasm32_wasi` platforms. The default wasm32 target model uses
`wasm32-unknown-unknown`, freestanding compile/link flags, imported
linear memory, no entry point, and local-sync as the only default HAL
driver.
* A `--config=wasm32_wasi` variant for targets that need
wasi-libc/libc++ behavior such as gtest/gbenchmark-oriented smoke
coverage.
* CMake wasm32 toolchain files mirroring the Bazel target model,
including deterministic wasi-sdk download/cache handling under the build
directory and the same freestanding compile/link flags.
* `iree_wasm_cc_library`, `iree_wasm_entry`, `iree_wasm_cc_binary`, and
`iree_wasm_cc_test` rules/macros for Bazel and CMake. C libraries can
declare JavaScript companion modules in their deps, binaries collect
them transitively, and the bundler emits a single `.mjs` entry point
beside the `.wasm` binary.
* A freestanding wasm libc shim: C headers, dlmalloc-backed allocation,
`sbrk` over `memory.grow`, string/ctype/strtol/stdio/stdlib/unistd
support, and a small `iree_syscall` JavaScript import module for
stdout/stderr, clock, exit, and assertion failure paths.
* Hooks for embedders to bring their own allocator or libc instead of
IREE's defaults. Bazel exposes the generic `--config=custom_allocator`
and `--config=wasm_custom_libc`; CMake exposes `IREE_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM`,
`IREE_WASM_BUILD_IREE_LIBC`, and `IREE_WASM_LIBC_INCLUDE_DIR`.
* JavaScript async proactor support under
`runtime/src/iree/async/platform/js/`. The C proactor owns token tables
and completion dispatch; JavaScript owns the event-loop integration,
Worker/inline entry points, completion ring plumbing, and import modules
used by browser or Node hosts.
* Runtime platform tightening for wasm: target-platform detection,
disabled unsafe synchronization, no threading by default, wasm-safe
time/CSPRNG/sysfs fallbacks, local topology stubs, and build-system
selection of the JS proactor where appropriate.
* Smoke tests for the wasm toolchain, the JS bundler, the JS proactor,
and the token table used to track externally completed operations.
* A small CMake-based `runtime_wasm` CI job that build-checks
representative wasm32 runtime targets with ccache, including a final
wasm link of the real `samples/hal/hello` runtime sample, without

Run the Bazel bundler smoke test under Node:

      --config=wasm32_wasi \

Build the CMake runtime wasm subset used by CI:

letting unsupported combinations look accidentally buildable.

not need VMVX or dynamic executable loading, and enabling VMVX today

boundary where they are introduced. Applications with an existing libc

build-regeneration paths while rebasing onto the current landing stack:

    cmake -G Ninja -B build-wasm-hello-test -S . \
      -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=build_tools/cmake/wasm32.cmake \

-DIREE_WASI_SDK_ROOT=./build-wasm-targeted/wasi-sdk/wasi-sdk-30.0-x86_64-linux

      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache \
      -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache \
      -DIREE_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION_PROFILE=size \
      -DIREE_ENABLE_LLD=ON

      --target \
        iree_wasm_libc \
        iree_samples_hal_hello_hello \
        iree_async_platform_js_proactor \
        iree_hal_drivers_local_sync_sync_driver \
      -- -k 0

    file build-wasm-hello-test/samples/hal/hello/hello

    llvm-readobj \
      --symbols build-wasm-hello-test/samples/hal/hello/hello

    iree-bazel-build \
      --config=wasm32 \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:smoke_test \
      //build_tools/wasm/test:bundler_test_bundle \
      //runtime/src/iree/base:base \
      //runtime/src/iree/async/platform/js:proactor \
      //runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/local_sync:sync_driver

module. `llvm-readobj` shows IREE libc functions such as `malloc`,

libc syscall shim.

yet: it currently reaches host generator/tooling targets such as

commit_message:
[Python] Preserve device-local buffer uploads (#24444)

Problem:
- Python ndarray arguments and `asdevicearray` uploads requested
device-local memory, but also requested `IREE_HAL_BUFFER_USAGE_MAPPING`
and forced `IREE_HAL_MEMORY_TYPE_HOST_VISIBLE` in `AllocateBufferCopy`.
- `IREE_HAL_BUFFER_USAGE_MAPPING` means the final HAL buffer may be
mapped by the host; it is not required for uploading host data into a
device buffer.
- On CUDA and other discrete GPU backends, requiring host-visible
mapping can prevent the allocator from choosing true device-local
memory.

Fix:
- Allocate buffer copies with the requested memory type instead of
forcing host-visible memory.
- Drop mapping usage from implicit ndarray and `asdevicearray` uploads,
so the default path creates device-local dispatch buffers.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Drop the power-of-two cap on `chooseUnrolling`.

`chooseUnrolling` previously enumerated `intrinsics_m` / `intrinsics_n`
through powers of two. There's no real reason for that — within the
register budget, the cost model can pick any factor.

Looking ahead: some intrinsics may eventually want the unroll factor
on a particular dim to be a multiple of some target-specific number —
Arm scalar-by-element FMA forms are an example, where the scalar is
a lane of a vector register, so covering whole vector registers is
more efficient. But even there it's not a strict preference: narrow
matmuls (e.g. matrix-vector) are better off avoiding the padding
that imposing that multiple would force. So a simple per-intrinsic
"preferred multiple" doesn't capture it. We'll come back to this when
we have a concrete need.

Lit-test fallout: relaxing pow2 lets the cost model land on better
non-pow2 unrolls in some cases the existing tests pin (e.g.
`materialize_encoding_x86_64.mlir`'s dynamic-N AVX-512 case now picks
`intrinsics_m = 29` instead of 16 — saturating the zmm register file
much more tightly, and at higher arithmetic intensity per the
existing scoring formula). CHECK lines updated to the new values.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>
name: pre-commit

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Support distinct LHS/RHS types in e2e matmul test framework.

The framework so far only generated symmetric-type matmuls (LHS and
RHS of the same type via `--lhs_rhs_type`). This generalizes it to
support `--lhs` and `--rhs` separately so we can test asymmetric-type
intrinsics like the upcoming x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd (LHS=ui8,
RHS=i8 → ACC=i32).

- `generate_e2e_matmul_tests.py`: replace `--lhs_rhs_type` with the
  per-operand `--lhs` / `--rhs` pair (legacy form still accepted; the
  CLI requires exactly one form). Adds a `ui8` choice. Plumbing for
  separate `lhs_type`/`rhs_type` is threaded through `generate()` /
  `generate_function()` / `generate_call()`.
- `generate_code.py`: emit a `linalg.generic` (with `arith.extui` /
  `arith.extsi` widening) when LHS != RHS or an operand is unsigned;
  buffer-view printing uses the `ui8` HAL element type for unsigned
  operands.
- `iree-e2e-matmul-test.cc`: new
  `REFERENCE_MATMUL(uint8_t, int8_t, int32_t, int32_t)` reference and
  matching dispatch arm for `IREE_HAL_ELEMENT_TYPE_UINT_8` LHS /
  signed-i8 RHS.

New test `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` exercises the
generated ui8/i8 matmul through the data-tiling + inner-tiled
pipeline. No matching hardware MMA intrinsic exists yet (this commit
is purely framework), so it only runs on the `generic` CPU variant
and falls through to the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA. A
follow-up PR adds the vpdpbusd MMA and an `avx512vnni` variant.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>

[Codegen][CPU] Support distinct LHS/RHS types in e2e matmul test framework.

The framework so far only generated symmetric-type matmuls (LHS and
RHS of the same type via `--lhs_rhs_type`). This generalizes it to
support `--lhs` and `--rhs` separately so we can test asymmetric-type
intrinsics like the upcoming x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd (LHS=ui8,
RHS=i8 → ACC=i32).

- `generate_e2e_matmul_tests.py`: replace `--lhs_rhs_type` with the
  per-operand `--lhs` / `--rhs` pair (legacy form still accepted; the
  CLI requires exactly one form). Adds a `ui8` choice. Plumbing for
  separate `lhs_type`/`rhs_type` is threaded through `generate()` /
  `generate_function()` / `generate_call()`.
- `generate_code.py`: emit a `linalg.generic` (with `arith.extui` /
  `arith.extsi` widening) when LHS != RHS or an operand is unsigned;
  buffer-view printing uses the `ui8` HAL element type for unsigned
  operands.
- `iree-e2e-matmul-test.cc`: new
  `REFERENCE_MATMUL(uint8_t, int8_t, int32_t, int32_t)` reference and
  matching dispatch arm for `IREE_HAL_ELEMENT_TYPE_UINT_8` LHS /
  signed-i8 RHS.

New test `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` exercises the
generated ui8/i8 matmul through the data-tiling + inner-tiled
pipeline. No matching hardware MMA intrinsic exists yet (this commit
is purely framework), so it only runs on the `generic` CPU variant
and falls through to the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA. A
follow-up PR adds the vpdpbusd MMA and an `avx512vnni` variant.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Drop the power-of-two cap on `chooseUnrolling`.

`chooseUnrolling` previously enumerated `intrinsics_m` / `intrinsics_n`
through powers of two. There's no real reason for that — within the
register budget, the cost model can pick any factor.

Looking ahead: some intrinsics may eventually want the unroll factor
on a particular dim to be a multiple of some target-specific number —
Arm scalar-by-element FMA forms are an example, where the scalar is
a lane of a vector register, so covering whole vector registers is
more efficient. But even there it's not a strict preference: narrow
matmuls (e.g. matrix-vector) are better off avoiding the padding
that imposing that multiple would force. So a simple per-intrinsic
"preferred multiple" doesn't capture it. We'll come back to this when
we have a concrete need.

Lit-test fallout: relaxing pow2 lets the cost model land on better
non-pow2 unrolls in some cases the existing tests pin (e.g.
`materialize_encoding_x86_64.mlir`'s dynamic-N AVX-512 case now picks
`intrinsics_m = 29` instead of 16 — saturating the zmm register file
much more tightly, and at higher arithmetic intensity per the
existing scoring formula). CHECK lines updated to the new values.

Progress towards #24323.

through powers of two. There's no real reason for that — within the
register budget, the cost model can pick any factor.

Looking ahead: some intrinsics may eventually want the unroll factor
on a particular dim to be a multiple of some target-specific number —
Arm scalar-by-element FMA forms are an example, where the scalar is
a lane of a vector register, so covering whole vector registers is
more efficient. But even there it's not a strict preference: narrow
matmuls (e.g. matrix-vector) are better off avoiding the padding
that imposing that multiple would force. So a simple per-intrinsic
"preferred multiple" doesn't capture it. We'll come back to this when
we have a concrete need.

Lit-test fallout: relaxing pow2 lets the cost model land on better
non-pow2 unrolls in some cases the existing tests pin (e.g.
`materialize_encoding_x86_64.mlir`'s dynamic-N AVX-512 case now picks
`intrinsics_m = 29` instead of 16 — saturating the zmm register file
much more tightly, and at higher arithmetic intensity per the
existing scoring formula). CHECK lines updated to the new values.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Drop the power-of-two cap on `chooseUnrolling`.

`chooseUnrolling` previously enumerated `intrinsics_m` / `intrinsics_n`
through powers of two. There's no real reason for that — within the
register budget, the cost model can pick any factor.

Looking ahead: some intrinsics may eventually want the unroll factor
on a particular dim to be a multiple of some target-specific number —
Arm scalar-by-element FMA forms are an example, where the scalar is
a lane of a vector register, so covering whole vector registers is
more efficient. But even there it's not a strict preference: narrow
matmuls (e.g. matrix-vector) are better off avoiding the padding
that imposing that multiple would force. So a simple per-intrinsic
"preferred multiple" doesn't capture it. We'll come back to this when
we have a concrete need.

Lit-test fallout: relaxing pow2 lets the cost model land on better
non-pow2 unrolls in some cases the existing tests pin (e.g.
`materialize_encoding_x86_64.mlir`'s dynamic-N AVX-512 case now picks
`intrinsics_m = 29` instead of 16 — saturating the zmm register file
much more tightly, and at higher arithmetic intensity per the
existing scoring formula). CHECK lines updated to the new values.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Support distinct LHS/RHS types in e2e matmul test framework.

The framework so far only generated symmetric-type matmuls (LHS and
RHS of the same type via `--lhs_rhs_type`). This generalizes it to
support `--lhs` and `--rhs` separately so we can test asymmetric-type
intrinsics like the upcoming x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd (LHS=ui8,
RHS=i8 → ACC=i32).

- `generate_e2e_matmul_tests.py`: replace `--lhs_rhs_type` with the
  per-operand `--lhs` / `--rhs` pair (legacy form still accepted; the
  CLI requires exactly one form). Adds a `ui8` choice. Plumbing for
  separate `lhs_type`/`rhs_type` is threaded through `generate()` /
  `generate_function()` / `generate_call()`.
- `generate_code.py`: emit a `linalg.generic` (with `arith.extui` /
  `arith.extsi` widening) when LHS != RHS or an operand is unsigned;
  buffer-view printing uses the `ui8` HAL element type for unsigned
  operands.
- `iree-e2e-matmul-test.cc`: new
  `REFERENCE_MATMUL(uint8_t, int8_t, int32_t, int32_t)` reference and
  matching dispatch arm for `IREE_HAL_ELEMENT_TYPE_UINT_8` LHS /
  signed-i8 RHS.

New test `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` exercises the
generated ui8/i8 matmul through the data-tiling + inner-tiled
pipeline. No matching hardware MMA intrinsic exists yet (this commit
is purely framework), so it only runs on the `generic` CPU variant
and falls through to the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA. A
follow-up PR adds the vpdpbusd MMA and an `avx512vnni` variant.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Add x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd MMA intrinsic.

Adds `vpdpbusd` — the AVX-512-VNNI byte dot-product — as a data-tiled
MMA intrinsic. It is the first asymmetric MMA: the first byte source
is unsigned, the second is signed, so the natural and swapped
orientations need different arg-routing at the call site (unlike the
LHS/RHS-symmetric FMA / dpbf16ps / vpdpwssd / pmaddw already
supported).

Two new enum values, `MMA_X86_AVX512VNNI_1x16x4_I32_UI8_I8` and its
M↔N-swapped sibling `MMA_X86_AVX512VNNI_16x1x4_I32_I8_UI8`, both
lower to `llvm.x86.avx512.vpdpbusd.512`. The swapped lowering flips
its (lhs, rhs) call args so the unsigned operand still lands in the
first slot.

Signedness handling — per IREE convention, vector tile types in IR are
signless, with the signed/unsigned distinction carried on the
encoding's `element_types`. `getABCElementTypes(intrinsic)` now
returns `ui8` where applicable, used by the cost model and validator
for matching against an encoding's `element_types`;
`getUndistributedTileTypes` strips the signedness when constructing
tile types. The validator and cost-model `getIntrinsicInfo` bypass
`getUndistributedTileTypes` and read shape + types straight from the
intrinsic via `getRowMajorTilesMNKShape` and `getABCElementTypes`,
which become public for that reason.

The prerequisite "distinct LHS/RHS types" PR added the
`e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` test on the `generic`
variant only; this commit adds the `avx512vnni` variant that
actually selects the new intrinsic.

Progress towards #24323.

[Codegen][CPU] Add x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd MMA intrinsic.

Adds `vpdpbusd` — the AVX-512-VNNI byte dot-product — as a data-tiled
MMA intrinsic. It is the first asymmetric MMA: the first byte source
is unsigned, the second is signed, so the natural and swapped
orientations need different arg-routing at the call site (unlike the
LHS/RHS-symmetric FMA / dpbf16ps / vpdpwssd / pmaddw already
supported).

M↔N-swapped sibling `MMA_X86_AVX512VNNI_16x1x4_I32_I8_UI8`, both
lower to `llvm.x86.avx512.vpdpbusd.512`. The swapped lowering flips
its (lhs, rhs) call args so the unsigned operand still lands in the
first slot.

signless, with the signed/unsigned distinction carried on the
encoding's `element_types`. `getABCElementTypes(intrinsic)` now
returns `ui8` where applicable, used by the cost model and validator
for matching against an encoding's `element_types`;
`getUndistributedTileTypes` strips the signedness when constructing
tile types. The validator and cost-model `getIntrinsicInfo` bypass
`getUndistributedTileTypes` and read shape + types straight from the
intrinsic via `getRowMajorTilesMNKShape` and `getABCElementTypes`,
which become public for that reason.

`e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` test on the `generic`
variant only; this commit adds the `avx512vnni` variant that
actually selects the new intrinsic.

[Codegen][CPU] Add x86 AVX-512 VNNI vpdpbusd MMA intrinsic.

Adds `vpdpbusd` — the AVX-512-VNNI byte dot-product — as a data-tiled
MMA intrinsic. It is the first asymmetric MMA: the first byte source
is unsigned, the second is signed, so the natural and swapped
orientations need different arg-routing at the call site (unlike the
LHS/RHS-symmetric FMA / dpbf16ps / vpdpwssd / pmaddw already
supported).

Two new enum values, `MMA_X86_AVX512VNNI_1x16x4_I32_UI8_I8` and its
M↔N-swapped sibling `MMA_X86_AVX512VNNI_16x1x4_I32_I8_UI8`, both
lower to `llvm.x86.avx512.vpdpbusd.512`. The swapped lowering flips
its (lhs, rhs) call args so the unsigned operand still lands in the
first slot.

Signedness handling — per IREE convention, vector tile types in IR are
signless, with the signed/unsigned distinction carried on the
encoding's `element_types`. `getABCElementTypes(intrinsic)` now
returns `ui8` where applicable, used by the cost model and validator
for matching against an encoding's `element_types`;
`getUndistributedTileTypes` strips the signedness when constructing
tile types. The validator and cost-model `getIntrinsicInfo` bypass
`getUndistributedTileTypes` and read shape + types straight from the
intrinsic via `getRowMajorTilesMNKShape` and `getABCElementTypes`,
which become public for that reason.

The prerequisite "distinct LHS/RHS types" PR added the
`e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_ui8_i8_i32` test on the `generic`
variant only; this commit adds the `avx512vnni` variant that
actually selects the new intrinsic.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Add e2e matmul tests for the inner_tiled lowering path.

Adds an `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_*` family that mirrors the
existing legacy-path `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_*` block (same type matrix:
i8/i32, f32/f32, f64/f64, f16/f16, f16/f32, bf16/bf16, bf16/f32; same
per-type x86 cpu-features variants; f64-demote guard; riscv/wasm
tags) but with `--iree-opt-data-tiling --iree-llvmcpu-enable-inner-tiled`.

Type×feature combos that match a hardware MMA intrinsic (e.g. f32/f32
on AVX2, bf16/f32 on AVX-512-BF16, i8/i32 on AVX-512-VNNI) exercise
the new `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` lowering; the rest fall through to
the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA (#24389), so this is a
correctness check on data-tiling-enabled compilation either way.

Shapes use the `default` set, except f64 (`small`, due to f64-demote
handling). The prerequisite pre-transposed-enum PR is what lets us
start at the full shape set rather than progressively widen.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>
name: pre-commit

Adds an `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_*` family that mirrors the
existing legacy-path `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_*` block (same type matrix:
i8/i32, f32/f32, f64/f64, f16/f16, f16/f32, bf16/bf16, bf16/f32; same
per-type x86 cpu-features variants; f64-demote guard; riscv/wasm
tags) but with `--iree-opt-data-tiling --iree-llvmcpu-enable-inner-tiled`.

Type×feature combos that match a hardware MMA intrinsic (e.g. f32/f32
on AVX2, bf16/f32 on AVX-512-BF16, i8/i32 on AVX-512-VNNI) exercise
the new `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` lowering; the rest fall through to
the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA (#24389), so this is a
correctness check on data-tiling-enabled compilation either way.

Shapes use the `default` set, except f64 (`small`, due to f64-demote
handling). The prerequisite pre-transposed-enum PR is what lets us
start at the full shape set rather than progressively widen.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>
name: runtime_tracing :: ubuntu-24.04-arm :: console

[Codegen][CPU] Add e2e matmul tests for the inner_tiled lowering path.

Adds an `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_inner_tiled_*` family that mirrors the
existing legacy-path `e2e_matmul_cpu_dt_*` block (same type matrix:
i8/i32, f32/f32, f64/f64, f16/f16, f16/f32, bf16/bf16, bf16/f32; same
per-type x86 cpu-features variants; f64-demote guard; riscv/wasm
tags) but with `--iree-opt-data-tiling --iree-llvmcpu-enable-inner-tiled`.

Type×feature combos that match a hardware MMA intrinsic (e.g. f32/f32
on AVX2, bf16/f32 on AVX-512-BF16, i8/i32 on AVX-512-VNNI) exercise
the new `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` lowering; the rest fall through to
the type-polymorphic generic-scalar MMA (#24389), so this is a
correctness check on data-tiling-enabled compilation either way.

Shapes use the `default` set, except f64 (`small`, due to f64-demote
handling). The prerequisite pre-transposed-enum PR is what lets us
start at the full shape set rather than progressively widen.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>
name: Test AMD MI355 / test_mi355

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Run HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes before vector lowering.

Mirrors the GPU pipeline (`buildLLVMGPUCodegenPassPipeline` adds this
pass right before `UnrollToIntrinsicsPass`). Before this change, on
CPU the reshape ops left around `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` sat
between the K-reduction loop's `scf.for` iter args and the op's
accumulator operand, so the per-tile `HoistableConversionOp` pairs
that the inner_tiled lowering wraps around its ACC
distribute/reassemble couldn't satisfy
`HoistConversionFromLoopPattern`'s strict iter-arg match. They
failed to hoist, got inlined in place, and
`EliminateHoistableConversions` fired a `hoistable_conversion was
not hoisted or cancelled; inlining in place` remark on every CPU
matmul build using the inner_tiled path.

Running `HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes` before
`LLVMCPUVirtualVectorLoweringPass` wraps the prefix/suffix reshape
ops (transpose, shape_cast, broadcast) around the inner_tiled as
`acc_reshape_to_intrinsic` / `acc_reshape_from_intrinsic` hoistable
conversions and runs the elimination over them. The reshapes hoist
out of the K loop, the inner_tiled's accumulator is fed directly by
the iter arg, and the per-tile conversion pairs emitted later in
the vector lowering see direct iter-arg inputs and hoist cleanly.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>

commit_message:
[Codegen] Skip swizzle transpose when permutation is a no-op modulo unit dims.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Run HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes before vector lowering.

Mirrors the GPU pipeline (`buildLLVMGPUCodegenPassPipeline` adds this
pass right before `UnrollToIntrinsicsPass`). Before this change, on
CPU the reshape ops left around `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` sat
between the K-reduction loop's `scf.for` iter args and the op's
accumulator operand, so the per-tile `HoistableConversionOp` pairs
that the inner_tiled lowering wraps around its ACC
distribute/reassemble couldn't satisfy
`HoistConversionFromLoopPattern`'s strict iter-arg match. They
failed to hoist, got inlined in place, and
`EliminateHoistableConversions` fired a `hoistable_conversion was
not hoisted or cancelled; inlining in place` remark on every CPU
matmul build using the inner_tiled path.

Running `HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes` before
`LLVMCPUVirtualVectorLoweringPass` wraps the prefix/suffix reshape
ops (transpose, shape_cast, broadcast) around the inner_tiled as
`acc_reshape_to_intrinsic` / `acc_reshape_from_intrinsic` hoistable
conversions and runs the elimination over them. The reshapes hoist
out of the K loop, the inner_tiled's accumulator is fed directly by
the iter arg, and the per-tile conversion pairs emitted later in
the vector lowering see direct iter-arg inputs and hoist cleanly.

Progress towards #24323.

[Codegen][CPU] Run HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes before vector lowering.

Mirrors the GPU pipeline (`buildLLVMGPUCodegenPassPipeline` adds this
pass right before `UnrollToIntrinsicsPass`). Before this change, on
CPU the reshape ops left around `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` sat
between the K-reduction loop's `scf.for` iter args and the op's
accumulator operand, so the per-tile `HoistableConversionOp` pairs
that the inner_tiled lowering wraps around its ACC
distribute/reassemble couldn't satisfy
`HoistConversionFromLoopPattern`'s strict iter-arg match. They
failed to hoist, got inlined in place, and
`EliminateHoistableConversions` fired a `hoistable_conversion was
not hoisted or cancelled; inlining in place` remark on every CPU
matmul build using the inner_tiled path.

Running `HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes` before
`LLVMCPUVirtualVectorLoweringPass` wraps the prefix/suffix reshape
ops (transpose, shape_cast, broadcast) around the inner_tiled as
`acc_reshape_to_intrinsic` / `acc_reshape_from_intrinsic` hoistable
conversions and runs the elimination over them. The reshapes hoist
out of the K loop, the inner_tiled's accumulator is fed directly by
the iter arg, and the per-tile conversion pairs emitted later in
the vector lowering see direct iter-arg inputs and hoist cleanly.

Progress towards #24323.

Signed-off-by: Benoit Jacob <jacob.benoit.1@gmail.com>

commit_message:
[Codegen] Skip swizzle transpose when permutation is a no-op modulo unit dims.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen] Skip swizzle transpose when permutation is a no-op modulo unit dims.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen][CPU] Run HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes before vector lowering.

Mirrors the GPU pipeline (`buildLLVMGPUCodegenPassPipeline` adds this
pass right before `UnrollToIntrinsicsPass`). Before this change, on
CPU the reshape ops left around `iree_codegen.inner_tiled` sat
between the K-reduction loop's `scf.for` iter args and the op's
accumulator operand, so the per-tile `HoistableConversionOp` pairs
that the inner_tiled lowering wraps around its ACC
distribute/reassemble couldn't satisfy
`HoistConversionFromLoopPattern`'s strict iter-arg match. They
failed to hoist, got inlined in place, and
`EliminateHoistableConversions` fired a `hoistable_conversion was
not hoisted or cancelled; inlining in place` remark on every CPU
matmul build using the inner_tiled path.

Running `HoistInnerTiledAccReshapes` before
`LLVMCPUVirtualVectorLoweringPass` wraps the prefix/suffix reshape
ops (transpose, shape_cast, broadcast) around the inner_tiled as
`acc_reshape_to_intrinsic` / `acc_reshape_from_intrinsic` hoistable
conversions and runs the elimination over them. The reshapes hoist
out of the K loop, the inner_tiled's accumulator is fed directly by
the iter arg, and the per-tile conversion pairs emitted later in
the vector lowering see direct iter-arg inputs and hoist cleanly.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen] Skip swizzle transpose when permutation is a no-op modulo unit dims.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[Codegen] Skip swizzle transpose when permutation is a no-op modulo unit dims.

The set_encoding pack lowering (and symmetrically the unset_encoding
unpack) currently always emits

  linalg.pack → tensor.expand_shape → linalg.transpose

to apply the swizzle's `permutation` to the packed inner tile. For
many swizzles the permutation only reorders unit dims relative to
non-unit dims (e.g. the generic-scalar 1×1×1 MMA ACC swizzle has
`expandShape = [[CrossIntrinsic(M), Internal(1)], [CrossIntrinsic(N),
Internal(1)]]` with `permutation = [0, 2, 1, 3]` — swapping the
`Internal(1)` placeholders past the `CrossIntrinsic` non-unit dims).
The linearized memory layout of the unpermuted and permuted shapes
is identical there, so the `linalg.transpose` is a no-op in terms of
data movement.

Add `isSwizzlePermutationLayoutNoOp`, a predicate that detects this
case (the permutation, restricted to non-unit source dims, is
order-preserving), and `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation`, which — when
the fold is expressible as a single reshape — builds a reassociation
that drops the `linalg.transpose`: the `tensor.expand_shape` (pack
side) / `tensor.collapse_shape` (unpack side) is instead given a
reassociation that lands directly on the permuted shape, partitioning
the permuted inner dims into contiguous slices matching the pack's
`innerTileSizes` one-to-one. Fall through to the existing expand +
transpose lowering when the permutation actually reorders non-unit
dims — the gfx950 scaled-matmul case for instance, where the
permutation moves a size-16 dim past two size-4 dims, must keep the
transpose — or when the layout-no-op result still isn't a single
reshape (a later group's non-unit dim positioned before an earlier
group's content; e.g. data-tiled i8 generic matmul with an all-unit
M group swapped past N's size-7 non-unit dim).

The folded reshape still carries the swizzle's unit dims: the
permuted inner shape is the materialized encoding type fixed by
`getEncodingInfo`, which dialect conversion requires the replacement
value to match exactly — dropping unit dims is not a local choice
here. Hence `getSwizzleFoldedReassociation` only picks a reassociation
reaching that already-fixed shape; whether the materialized type
should carry unit dims at all is a separate, cross-cutting question.

This was motivated by a separate bug in
`hoistOneStaticallyBoundAllocation` (#24483): under dynamic shapes
the intermediate `tensor.empty` between the pack and the transpose
bufferizes to a stack alloca whose size comes from
`ValueBoundsConstraintSet::computeConstantBound` on the dynamic dim,
which for a workload-ordinal dim with only the default `index` umax
constraint (2^53 - 1) produces a ~2^52-element static alloca,
overflows i64 stride math, and lowers to `llvm.alloca poison`.
Eliminating the intermediate via this fast path sidesteps the bug
for the cases that hit this path; the hoist bug is real and the
fix here is in addition to fixing it at the source.

Progress towards #24323.

commit_message:
[VectorDistribute] Distribute `vector.scan` across subgroups (#24475)

Follow-up to https://github.com/iree-org/iree/pull/24312 to enable
distribution of associative scan operations across multiple subgroups in
a workgroup.

In contrast to reduction operations which produce a uniform result,
scans have one result per input element plus a second result for the
overall outcome. Therefore, the distribution is different from e.g.
`multi_reduction`.

Also adds E2E tests for the associative scan operation.

This is part of https://github.com/iree-org/iree/issues/24186.

Assisted-by: Claude Code and Codex

---------

Signed-off-by: Lukas Sommer <lukas.sommer@amd.com>

commit_message:
[Vulkan] HAL Rewrite (#24459)

This should be compatible with old VMFBs. I expect some platforms to
possibly need feature backfill or compatibility support but our testing
story is too thin to know yet. The big shift here is baselining on
Vulkan 1.3. With a bit of extra work we could stretch back to 1.2 with
extensions.

---

This PR replaces the legacy Vulkan HAL with a new implementation built
around the current HAL queue contract, native Vulkan command recording,
explicit feature negotiation, buffer-device-address dispatch, direct
transfer/file paths, and HAL-native profiling.

The old driver worked (and was some of the oldest IREE code, written
before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions
that do not map well to modern IREE workloads. In particular, it did not
give us a clean way to model asynchronous queue frontiers, reusable
command-buffer replay, file/transfer operations, BDA dispatch, or
backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

The new driver has two goals:

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.
- Make the optimized Vulkan path descriptor-free, replayable,
observable, and aligned with the same command-buffer model used by newer
HAL backends.

## Driver Architecture

The implementation is organized around explicit ownership boundaries:

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and
queue-family description.
- `logical_device.*` owns logical-device creation, queue selection,
topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.
- `queue.*` owns queue submission, timeline epochs, dependency
resolution, native command-buffer allocation, asynchronous completion,
staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline
creation, descriptor ABI metadata, BDA ABI metadata, raw BDA executable
support, global lookup, and per-pipeline dispatch metadata.

Unsupported cases are rejected at the boundary where they are
discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

## Queue Model

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue
epochs. Each selected queue lane tracks accepted submissions,
signal/wait frontiers, completion state, and pending cleanup. HAL
semaphore dependencies are resolved through the queue path without
assuming FIFO submission order.

Queue submission supports:

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

This replaces the old split between synchronous direct operations and
special driver-side helper paths. Queue work now enters through one
scheduling model and retires through one completion model.

## Executable And Dispatch ABIs

The driver supports both Vulkan executable ABIs:

- `vulkan-spirv-fb`, the descriptor ABI, for compatibility with existing
descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for
descriptor-free dispatch through a device-address binding table.

The descriptor ABI now uses `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` when the device
supports it and the pipeline layout fits the extension limits. That
removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

BDA is the primary performance path. The runtime publishes a compact
device-address binding table and the shader reads resource addresses
directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

## Device Compatibility

This rewrite intentionally raises the Vulkan baseline. The
driver-created instance requests Vulkan 1.3 by default, and
physical-device enumeration only accepts devices with:

- `apiVersion >= VK_API_VERSION_1_3`;
- `timelineSemaphore`;
- `scalarBlockLayout`;
- `synchronization2`;
- at least one compute-capable queue family.

That baseline is what lets the queue use timeline-semaphore epochs,
express barriers through synchronization2, and keep shader/storage
layouts consistent without carrying old synchronization and layout
compatibility paths. The target is Vulkan 1.3, not Vulkan 1.4; Vulkan
1.3 has been the stable modern Vulkan baseline since [January
2022](https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/versions.html#vulkan-13-features-breakdown).

`bufferDeviceAddress` is a second gate for the optimized BDA dispatch
ABI. A device can still use descriptor-ABI executables without BDA, but
`vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw` require BDA because
their binding table is a table of device addresses instead of descriptor
bindings.

Optional capabilities remain opportunistic:

- `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` accelerates the descriptor compatibility path
when available.
- `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` improves profile clock correlation when
available.
- external memory, host memory import, sparse binding, and sparse
residency are enabled only when the device and requested HAL features
require them.

As a rough ecosystem sanity check, the [Vulkan Hardware Database
`apiVersion`
distribution](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion)
reports Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4 in 24,376 of 44,893 submitted all-platform
reports (54.3%). The desktop slice is stronger: 12,446 of 19,758
[Windows
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=windows)
(63.0%) and 9,547 of 15,964 [Linux
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=linux)
(59.8%) are Vulkan 1.3+. Android is lower at 2,400 of 7,832 [Android
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=android)
(30.6%), which matches the fact that this rewrite is primarily aimed at
modern desktop/server Vulkan rather than old mobile Vulkan stacks.

The required feature bits are not the practical compatibility cliff
within the modern driver cohort: gpuinfo.org's all-platform [Vulkan 1.2
feature coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore12.php) and
[Vulkan 1.3 feature
coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.

## Command Buffers

HAL command buffers record structured Vulkan command records instead of
trying to expose old direct-command-buffer behavior through the HAL API.
During recording the driver accumulates:

- descriptor requirements for descriptor ABI replay;
- BDA publication byte requirements for BDA replay;
- retained resources for safe command-buffer lifetime;
- dispatch metadata required for profiling and native replay.

At queue execution time the command buffer is replayed into a native
`VkCommandBuffer`. BDA command buffers can use the native replay cache:
the cache keeps reusable native command buffers and BDA publication
storage per queue lane, skips publication when binding slots are
unchanged, and exposes
hits, misses, forks, bypasses, trims, peak instance count, and peak
publication bytes through `query_i64` counters under
`vulkan.queue.native_replay_cache`.

Descriptor command buffers currently bypass native replay caching
because their replayed Vulkan commands embed binding-table-dependent
descriptor state. This matches the old indirect-command-buffer shape:
the old driver recorded deferred HAL commands for binding-table command
buffers and materialized a native Vulkan command buffer during each
`queue_execute`. The rewrite keeps that compatibility contract, uses
push descriptors when available, and reserves resident native replay for
BDA command buffers where the command body is independent of the
execute-time binding table.

## Transfer And File Paths

Queue transfers are native Vulkan operations in the new driver. Fill,
update, and copy are recorded directly into Vulkan command buffers.
Unaligned fill and update edges are patched with driver-owned built-in
pipelines instead of falling through an emulated transfer layer.

File reads and writes use storage-buffer-backed files directly when
available. Host-backed files are staged through device-visible memory
and the async file path, keeping file operations on the same
queue/completion model as the rest of the driver.

## Profiling And Statistics

Profiling is built into the queue and command-buffer paths. The driver
records HAL executable metadata, command-buffer metadata, queue events,
queue device timestamps, and optional per-dispatch timestamp ranges
through the local HAL profile recorder used by `iree-profile`.

Timestamp query pools are queue-owned and cached. Calibrated timestamp
support is used when available to relate Vulkan device ticks to the HAL
profile timeline, and invalid calibrated ranges are marked instead of
forcing a bad clock fit.

The driver also exposes backend statistics through device queries,
including native replay cache behavior, BDA publication cache behavior,
and timestamp query cache behavior. These counters make performance
paths inspectable instead of requiring driver-internal debugging.

## Performance Characterization

The performance goal of the rewrite is simple: Vulkan command buffers
should be cheap to submit because the backend records native Vulkan work
once and replays that work directly. The benchmark rows below keep that
contract visible by separating host submit cost from end-to-end drain
cost:

- Submit-only rows time command-buffer replay and queue submission, with
the final completion wait outside the timed region.
- Submit + wait rows include the final completion wait and therefore
include driver and device drain behavior.

All rows are release Google Benchmark medians. The benchmark set
compares the old descriptor-set Vulkan HAL, the new
descriptor-compatible Vulkan path, the new BDA Vulkan dispatch ABI, and
AMDGPU AQL/PM4 command-buffer replay. Those are distinct mechanisms, so
the tables keep them separate instead of turning the result into a
single backend ranking.

### Vulkan Command-Buffer Replay

Homogeneous 10K-dispatch command-buffer replay:

| Path | ABI | Submit-only | Submit + wait | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Old Vulkan HAL | Descriptor sets | 5.139 ms | 5.609 ms | Deferred HAL
command buffer replayed into Vulkan and bound descriptor sets for every
dispatch. |
| New Vulkan HAL | Push descriptors | 2.072 ms | 5.257 ms | Descriptor
compatibility path avoids descriptor pool/set churn and cuts host replay
cost by 2.48x. |
| New Vulkan HAL | BDA | 12.361 us | 1.435 ms | Native BDA replay hits
the native replay cache and cuts host replay cost by 416x vs old Vulkan.
|

The descriptor row is the compatibility story: the new HAL is still
faster than old Vulkan when running the legacy descriptor ABI. The BDA
row is the design story: when the compiler targets the new ABI, replay
becomes one cached native command-buffer submission instead of a
per-dispatch descriptor-binding loop.

For command-buffer recording, the hot unvalidated/unretained path
remains close to the old implementation, and the default checked path is

[Vulkan] HAL Rewrite (#24459)

This should be compatible with old VMFBs. I expect some platforms to
possibly need feature backfill or compatibility support but our testing
story is too thin to know yet. The big shift here is baselining on
Vulkan 1.3. With a bit of extra work we could stretch back to 1.2 with
extensions.

---

This PR replaces the legacy Vulkan HAL with a new implementation built
around the current HAL queue contract, native Vulkan command recording,
explicit feature negotiation, buffer-device-address dispatch, direct
transfer/file paths, and HAL-native profiling.

The old driver worked (and was some of the oldest IREE code, written
before it was even open sourced!), but it grew around synchronous
submission, descriptor-set dispatch, and direct recording assumptions
that do not map well to modern IREE workloads. In particular, it did not
give us a clean way to model asynchronous queue frontiers, reusable
command-buffer replay, file/transfer operations, BDA dispatch, or
backend-visible profiling statistics without continuing to layer
compatibility paths on top of the old design.

The new driver has two goals:

- Keep descriptor ABI compatibility for existing Vulkan executables.
- Make the optimized Vulkan path descriptor-free, replayable,
observable, and aligned with the same command-buffer model used by newer
HAL backends.

## Driver Architecture

The implementation is organized around explicit ownership boundaries:

- `api.*` defines Vulkan HAL feature policy, extension names, and public
option translation.
- `physical_device.*` owns enumeration, device snapshots, baseline
validation, extension discovery, feature/property capture, and
queue-family description.
- `logical_device.*` owns logical-device creation, queue selection,
topology, allocator installation, executable-cache creation, file
import, and device queries.
- `queue.*` owns queue submission, timeline epochs, dependency
resolution, native command-buffer allocation, asynchronous completion,
staging, direct dispatch, transfer/file operation recording, profiling
timestamps, and replay cache statistics.
- `command_buffer.*` owns reusable HAL command-buffer storage, compact
command records, descriptor/BDA requirement accounting, resource
lifetime tracking, and native replay into `VkCommandBuffer`.
- `executable.*` owns Vulkan executable loading, SPIR-V module/pipeline
creation, descriptor ABI metadata, BDA ABI metadata, raw BDA executable
support, global lookup, and per-pipeline dispatch metadata.

Unsupported cases are rejected at the boundary where they are
discovered. The rewrite intentionally avoids silent fallbacks that would
hide missing Vulkan features or route hot paths through emulation.

## Queue Model

The new queue implementation uses Vulkan timeline semaphores as queue
epochs. Each selected queue lane tracks accepted submissions,
signal/wait frontiers, completion state, and pending cleanup. HAL
semaphore dependencies are resolved through the queue path without
assuming FIFO submission order.

Queue submission supports:

- execution barriers;
- queue allocation and deallocation;
- sparse binding;
- fill, update, copy, read, and write operations;
- direct dispatch;
- reusable command-buffer execute;
- file-backed staging;
- host callbacks.

This replaces the old split between synchronous direct operations and
special driver-side helper paths. Queue work now enters through one
scheduling model and retires through one completion model.

## Executable And Dispatch ABIs

The driver supports both Vulkan executable ABIs:

- `vulkan-spirv-fb`, the descriptor ABI, for compatibility with existing
descriptor-set storage-buffer executables.
- `vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw`, the BDA ABIs, for
descriptor-free dispatch through a device-address binding table.

The descriptor ABI now uses `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` when the device
supports it and the pipeline layout fits the extension limits. That
removes descriptor pool allocation and descriptor-set update overhead
from the descriptor compatibility path.

BDA is the primary performance path. The runtime publishes a compact
device-address binding table and the shader reads resource addresses
directly. Reusable command buffers can keep the native Vulkan command
body resident while only the published BDA table bytes change between
executions.

## Device Compatibility

This rewrite intentionally raises the Vulkan baseline. The
driver-created instance requests Vulkan 1.3 by default, and
physical-device enumeration only accepts devices with:

- `apiVersion >= VK_API_VERSION_1_3`;
- `timelineSemaphore`;
- `scalarBlockLayout`;
- `synchronization2`;
- at least one compute-capable queue family.

That baseline is what lets the queue use timeline-semaphore epochs,
express barriers through synchronization2, and keep shader/storage
layouts consistent without carrying old synchronization and layout
compatibility paths. The target is Vulkan 1.3, not Vulkan 1.4; Vulkan
1.3 has been the stable modern Vulkan baseline since [January
2022](https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/versions.html#vulkan-13-features-breakdown).

`bufferDeviceAddress` is a second gate for the optimized BDA dispatch
ABI. A device can still use descriptor-ABI executables without BDA, but
`vulkan-spirv-bda-v1` and `vulkan-spirv-bda-raw` require BDA because
their binding table is a table of device addresses instead of descriptor
bindings.

Optional capabilities remain opportunistic:

- `VK_KHR_push_descriptor` accelerates the descriptor compatibility path
when available.
- `VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps` improves profile clock correlation when
available.
- external memory, host memory import, sparse binding, and sparse
residency are enabled only when the device and requested HAL features
require them.

As a rough ecosystem sanity check, the [Vulkan Hardware Database
`apiVersion`
distribution](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion)
reports Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4 in 24,376 of 44,893 submitted all-platform
reports (54.3%). The desktop slice is stronger: 12,446 of 19,758
[Windows
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=windows)
(63.0%) and 9,547 of 15,964 [Linux
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=linux)
(59.8%) are Vulkan 1.3+. Android is lower at 2,400 of 7,832 [Android
reports](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/displaycoreproperty.php?name=apiversion&platform=android)
(30.6%), which matches the fact that this rewrite is primarily aimed at
modern desktop/server Vulkan rather than old mobile Vulkan stacks.

within the modern driver cohort: gpuinfo.org's all-platform [Vulkan 1.2
feature coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore12.php) and
[Vulkan 1.3 feature
coverage](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/listfeaturescore13.php) list
`timelineSemaphore` at 99.88%, `scalarBlockLayout` at 98.82%,
`synchronization2` at 99.82%, and `bufferDeviceAddress` at 98.47%. Treat
those numbers as [community-submitted device/report coverage rather than
market share](https://vulkan.gpuinfo.org/about.php), but they are useful
evidence that the meaningful bump is the Vulkan 1.3 driver baseline, not
an obscure optional-feature combination.
